title: Camp 4 close: the reed and the emperor
hook: seventy-five days with two books; next, the depths

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grammarian in the storm and the lion with no tail. Your line was hundreds more. Did you find a story we didn't read? Day two hundred thirty-one, the last day of camp four.

Seventy-five days ago, you picked up two books at once. One by a Persian poet in thirteenth-century Konya, dictated to a student late into the night. One by a Roman emperor, scribbled to himself in Greek in a tent by a frozen river. Two men who never met, a thousand years apart, who would have found each other strange. You've carried both, and kept them apart, and something of each has rubbed off. Today we close the camp and name what we found. Camp four close: the reed and the emperor.
screen: `TWO BOOKS, SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS.` → `KONYA, AND A TENT BY THE DANUBE.` → `THE REED AND THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Here are the camp's words, in the order we met them. Masnavi, Rumi's long book of stories, about twenty-five thousand couplets. Sufi, the Islamic mystical path he walked, and our promise to keep him whole, Quran, Prophet and all. Ney, the reed flute crying for the reedbed. Tawakkul, trust in God, with the camel still tied. Daimon, Marcus's divine spark within, to be honored and kept upright. Ghazal, the love poem signed with Shams' name. Sema, the turning, listening with the whole body. And Şeb-i Arus, the wedding night, a death kept as a meeting. Around those words, the two men gave us two great moods. From Rumi, longing. Everyone parted from their source wants to go back, and that ache isn't a malfunction; it's a direction. From Marcus, duty. Do the next thing in front of you, justly and kindly, without hurry, as if it were the last. Longing pulls you toward what you love. Duty keeps your feet on the ground where you are. They don't merge, and we won't pretend they're one teaching. But a person can carry both, the way you can carry a compass and a lantern. And now, the depths. Camp five is the last camp of this year. For seven weeks we'll visit the other doors on this app, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Catholicism, Islam and Sikhism, one first idea at a time, told the way each tradition tells itself. Then the Stoics, properly. Then what science can honestly say. It starts tomorrow with how to be a guest.
screen: `MASNAVI, SUFI, NEY, TAWAKKUL.` · `DAIMON, GHAZAL, SEMA, ŞEB-I ARUS.` · `FROM RUMI, LONGING; FROM MARCUS, DUTY.` · `NEXT: SEVEN VISITS, THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `LONGING AND DUTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with longing and with duty. Settle and breathe. First, longing. Let yourself feel what you most deeply want, the reed's ache, without fixing it. Let it be a direction. Then, duty. Name the one next thing in front of you today, small and plain. Let it be solid ground. Hold both, one in each hand, and breathe between them. The bell holds the time.
Camp four close. Seventy-five days with Rumi and Marcus: longing and duty, two books read side by side and never merged. Today's word.
Your line: longing and duty. Today, do one plain duty with a little of the reed's longing in it: the dishes, a report, a call home. Day two hundred thirty-one. Camp four is complete.

screen: `DAY 231 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW TO BE A GUEST.`

howItsDone: Readers who have finished a long reading of Rumi and Marcus often keep both books near: Rumi for longing and devotion, Marcus for daily duty, read a few lines at a time.

fork.setup: you've finished seventy-five days with two books. which one do you keep?
options: both, side by side: longing and duty.
fork.reveal: the camp's point was never to pick a winner: Rumi gives longing, Marcus gives duty, and a person can carry both without merging them.

what it means: a Sufi's longing for God and a Stoic's daily duty, each kept whole.
what a scholar hears: the Masnavi, dictated to Husam al-Din from about 1258; the Meditations, written in the 170s during the northern wars.
